note: Built incrementally from each case's verified extract; powers the merged Table of Authorities.

53127.name: Balram Kumawat v. Union of India & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Discussed principles of statutory interpretation including contextual reading, the rule of ex visceribus actus (construction of the statute as a whole), and the principle that narrow and pedantic literal construction may not always be given effect to fiscal or penal statutes, which must instead be interpreted having regard to the subject matter and object of the law. The Court cited this case for the proposition that purposive interpretation can apply even to penal statutes.

603736.name: State of West Bengal v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: Laid down the principle that the Court must ascertain the intention of the legislature by directing attention to the entire statute and comparing the clause to be construed with other parts of the law. This case was cited for the rule of contextual reading and ex visceribus actus.

995861.name: R.S. Raghunath v. State of Karnataka and Anr.

cited_by.proposition: Reiterated the principle that the clauses of a statute should be construed with reference to context and other provisions to make a consistent enactment. Applied the rule of ex visceribus actus.

A case dealing with interpretation of a definition using the word ‘means’ (‘member of his family’ under Tamil Nadu Rent Act). Despite ‘means’ seemingly limiting the definition to specified relatives, the Court held that a foster son could be included by purposive construction, observing that interpretation should aid the achievement of the Act’s purpose. Cited as a comparable example demonstrating that ‘means’ is not always exhaustive.

477582.name: Bhilai Rerollers & Ors. v. M.P. Electricity Board & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with a case where a consumer drew electricity in excess of contracted load. The Board had the right under the general conditions of supply to levy higher charges. The Court held that the Board was entitled to raise the demand because overdrawal of extra load throws out of gear the entire supply system, undermining its efficiency and efficacy and causing voltage fluctuations. The Court rejected the consumer’s challenge.

275403.name: Orissa State Electricity Board & Anr. v. IPI Steel Ltd. & Ors.

cited_by.proposition: Took a similar view to Bhilai Rerollers regarding cases of excess load of consumption.

93301.name: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Vishwa Caliber Builders Private Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Concerned whether the ombudsman had jurisdiction to regularize unauthorized electricity supply. The Court answered in the negative and held that consumption of electricity by the respondent beyond the sanctioned load amounted to unauthorized use of electrical energy, even where the excess arose from non-availability of infrastructure (transformer).

69408974.name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with interpretation of ‘unauthorized development’ under Section 31A of the Delhi Development Act, 1957. The Court held that development in violation of permission, approval, sanction, or conditions thereof constitutes unauthorized development. Used as an analogy to interpret ‘unauthorized use of electricity’ as use in violation of permission or authorization granted.

374797.name: Dr. S. Dutt v. State of U.P.

cited_by.proposition: Stated that a person who does anything with the intention to cause wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another is said to do that dishonestly. Cited for the meaning of ‘dishonest’ under Section 135 of the Electricity Act.

1885496.name: Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai

cited_by.proposition: Extensively discussed the scope of Article 226 jurisdiction and when alternative remedy does not bar the exercise of writ jurisdiction. Held that the power to issue prerogative writs is plenary and not limited by other constitutional provisions, and that the alternative remedy bar operates with exceptions, particularly where the order is wholly without jurisdiction, vires of an Act is challenged, or natural justice is violated.

1663246.name: Union of India v. State of Haryana

cited_by.proposition: Held that where a fundamental legal question requires determination (e.g., whether a particular transaction is a sale), the matter need not be put through the mill of statutory appeals in hierarchy but should be determined by the High Court as a question of law.

970048.name: State of A.P. v. National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Held that electricity is a movable good in that it can be transmitted, transferred, delivered, and possessed like any other movable property. This position established that electricity is not immovable property.

1887300.name: Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Haji Abdulgafur Haji Hussenbha
1887300.court: High Court (cited with approval by Supreme Court)

cited_by.proposition: Held (in the context of municipal taxes) that a municipal corporation, which had a charge on property by virtue of law for recovery of tax dues, could recover arrears of taxes from an auction purchaser who had become the owner of the property. The purchaser, who resisted recovery on grounds of lack of notice, was held liable because the charge arose by operation of law, not by notice.

101057776.name: Brihanmumbai Electric Supply & Transport Undertaking v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Held that the obligation of the distribution licensee to supply electricity to premises will begin only after the owner or occupier submits a completed application. The explanation to Section 43 clarifies that the application must be complete in all respects along with necessary documents showing payment of charges and compliances.

197296101.name: BSES Ltd. v. Tata Power Co. Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Held that the term “tariff” in the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998 is not defined in the Act and must be understood in common parlance as a schedule of standard prices or charges for categories of customers.

1312982.name: AI Champdany Industries Ltd. v. Official Liquidator

cited_by.proposition: Held that charges can be created by act of parties or by operation of law. A charge arising by operation of law does not require registration and arises automatically when a statute or regulation prescribes it.

1941195.name: India Thermal Power Ltd. v. State of M.P.

cited_by.treatment: Cited by appellant; distinguished by Court
cited_by.proposition: Held that a state cannot unilaterally impose conditions on electricity distribution that go beyond the statutory framework without violating principles of fairness and statutory construction.

1542937.name: Deputy Commercial Tax Officer, Park Town Division v. Sha Sukhraj Peerajee

cited_by.treatment: Cited by appellant; distinguished by Court
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the enforceability of demands made by tax authorities. Held that a demand or condition imposed must be grounded in statutory authority and cannot be arbitrary.

1703652.name: Jivendra Nath Kaul v. Collector/District Magistrate

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with statutory authority and delegation of legislative power. Held that regulations framed in exercise of delegated authority under a parent statute are valid and enforceable if the parent statute clearly authorizes such framing.

1324332.name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Hindustan Aluminium Corporation

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with state control and regulatory authority. Held that a state can exercise regulatory authority within the scope of powers conferred by statute.

223862.name: Jagdamba Paper Industries (P) Ltd. v. Haryana State Electricity Board

cited_by.proposition: Held that the conditions of supply stipulated by licensees or Boards have a statutory character.

1040803.name: Bihar State Electricity Board v. Parmeshwar Kumar Agarwala

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the statutory rights of electricity boards to enforce payment conditions and pursue remedies for non-payment.

1429681.name: Ferro Alloys Corp. Ltd. v. A.P. State Electricity Board

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the statutory authority of state electricity boards and their regulatory obligations.

1741134.name: Deepak Theatre v. State of Punjab

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with regulatory authority and conditions imposed in public utilities.

87528.name: K. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with statutory authority and regulatory conditions in the context of electricity distribution.

395434.name: PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the regulatory authority of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission and the statutory character of its orders.

62408831.name: V.S. Rice and Oil Mills v. State of Andhra Pradesh

cited_by.proposition: Held that “power to regulate carries with it full power over the thing subject to regulation and in absence of restrictive words, the power must be regarded as plenary over the entire subject.” This is a principle of interpreting regulatory authority.

4853151.name: Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Super & Stainless Hi Alloys Ltd.

cited_by.treatment: Reference order; present appeals arise from it
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the recovery of electricity dues from auction purchasers. The reference order dated 24 August 2006 in this case was the occasion for referring the batch of appeals to a 3-judge Bench for clarification of whether electricity dues constitute a charge on property.

97950877.name: Maharashtra State Electricity Board v. Ecto Spinners

cited_by.treatment: Cited; issue decided in present judgment
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with electricity dues recovery and the liability of new owners of premises.

1102044.name: U.T. Chandigarh Administration v. Amarjeet Singh

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with property transfers in a financial corporation context and the rights and liabilities of subsequent purchasers in auctions conducted by financial corporations.

764540.name: M/s Swastic Industries v. Maharashtra State Electricity Board

cited_by.treatment: Cited; issue decided in present judgment
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the recovery of electricity dues and the applicability of conditions of supply to new owners.

1873931.name: Kusumam Hotels Pvt. Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board

cited_by.treatment: Cited; issue decided in present judgment
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the recovery of electricity dues from subsequent purchasers of premises in Kerala context.

1477095.name: Adoni Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the rule of ejusdem generis in the context of electricity regulations. The rule requires that when a statute enumerates specific items followed by general words, the general words must be confined to items of the same class as those enumerated.

cited_by.treatment: Cited in support of interpretation principles
cited_by.proposition: Dealt with principles of statutory interpretation, including the interpretation of regulatory authority.

277738.name: Mangalore Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. The Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the characterization of electricity dues and the statutory status of electricity supply entities.

369141.name: Tata Motors Ltd. v. Pharmaceutical Products of India Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with principles of statutory interpretation and the distinction between different legal concepts when different words are used.
Dealt with the enforceability of statutory claims and the protection of legitimate statutory interests.

914491.name: UP State Electricity Board v. Hari Shankar Jain

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with the statutory authority of state electricity boards and their power to impose conditions for supply.

885483.name: KSL & Industries Ltd. v. Arihant Threads Ltd.

cited_by.proposition: Dealt with statutory rights and the enforcement of conditions arising by operation of law.

160269658.name: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board

cited_by.proposition: Held that a charge on assets securing electricity dues need not rest on an express provision of the Electricity Act, 2003 but can be created by properly framed regulations authorized under the parent statute; and that such a charge can be invoked to prevent transfer of assets by a subsequent purchaser.
